objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK by the June deadline that the Council can approve, so the modification proceeds on an agreed rather than contested basis

Secure UK tariff-free access at a level defensible as 'substantially equivalent' compensation, ideally through an enlarged TRQ and/or a UK country-specific allocation, while preserving the 50% out-of-quota bound rate as the core of the measure
Prevent a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA dispute and any coordinated disapplication of FTA commitments in retaliation — this is the scenario I most need to avoid
Use the FTA disapplication provision as tradable negotiating currency: it was included to create headroom, and softening or carving out the UK from it is my cheapest major concession
Link UK concessions on treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard (where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas) into the overall balance
Protect my long-term working relationship with the UK counterpart and the EU's standing in Geneva committees, which outlast this file
Keep the process clean and legally sound so the Article XXVIII modification cannot be challenged on procedural grounds
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement both capitals accept within four rounds, delivering the UK a meaningful country-specific share of an enlarged quota plus a carve-out or softening of the FTA disapplication, in exchange for UK acceptance of the 50% bound rate, no FTA dispute, and no erosion of EU quota treatment under the UK's safeguard — all reportable to Brussels as within a plausible mandate. Partial success: no settlement but no joint FTA dispute and a preserved working relationship, leaving the EU free to proceed as notified. Failure: the UK walks, coordinates with Japan and Korea on a joint FTA dispute, and I am left managing retaliation and reputational damage across multiple files in Geneva while Brussels blames the process rather than the politics.
declaration.approach: Open by establishing process credibility: acknowledge the UK's principal supplying interest, commit to genuine negotiation, and set a timeline to June. Do not table concessions early — first draw out the UK's priorities (volume vs allocation method vs FTA treatment) and make them spend capital naming their asks. Hold the 400,000t global first-come-first-served opening as the notified position and make any movement visibly conditional. My natural package is: larger TRQ plus a UK country-specific allocation (administered by licensing, which the UK industry will prefer for certainty) plus UK carve-out from the FTA disapplication — but I trade these one at a time, extracting in return (a) UK confirmation it will not join any FTA dispute action, (b) preservation of EU country-specific quotas under the UK safeguard, and (c) UK acceptance of the 50% rate and enforcement/circumvention provisions. I will keep Turkey, Korea, India and Japan visibly separate from the UK track and quietly signal to the UK that a bilateral settlement is its best protection against being lumped in with higher-volume claimants. Throughout, I report to Brussels honestly about what is achievable and frame recommendations so the Council sees a negotiated outcome as cheaper than contested retaliation.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (UK Mission, working for DBT)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access: a large UK country-specific quota (they will anchor near their 2.4Mt export average, or at least well above 400kt), licensing rather than first-come-first-served, withdrawal of the FTA disapplication, product carve-outs for their concentrated lines, and a review clause. They will also defend EU quota treatment under their own safeguard and may hint at joining Japan/Korea in a dispute as leverage.

parties.who: Brussels / Commission DG TRADE and the Council (via Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A concluded process by June, no precedent that undermines the permanent steel regime, a TRQ that steel-producing member states can live with, and no unravelling of the FTA disapplication architecture for other partners. Steel-consuming member states will quietly welcome generous UK access; producers will resist it. They gave no settlement figure, so they want a defensible package, not a specific number.

parties.who: Japan and Korea
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own Article XXVIII compensation, and leverage — hence the whispered effort to recruit the UK into a joint FTA dispute. They want the FTA disapplication abandoned or narrowed, and they watch the UK deal as a floor for their own.

parties.who: Turkey and India
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Compensation reflecting their larger (Turkey) or substantial (India) supply volumes; likely to resist any UK country-specific allocation that shrinks the residual global quota available to them.

parties.who: UK domestic steel industry and DBT ministers
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed volumes into the EU market (75% of UK exports), predictability through licensing and country-specific shares, and a political win they can present to steel communities — which makes them press their Geneva seat hard against any first-come-first-served global quota.

parties.who: EU steel industry and steel-producing member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A tight TRQ, high out-of-quota protection retained, strong anti-circumvention enforcement, and scepticism toward any UK carve-out from the FTA disapplication.

objectives: Secure the Article XXVIII modification on terms that preserve the legal architecture of the steel import regime: a high bound out-of-quota rate (50%) and a controlled TRQ that significantly reduces import volumes
Reach agreement with the UK within the negotiating window so the Council can vote on the implementing act in June as scheduled
Retain the legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions for non-EEA partners, including the UK, so preferential access cannot be stacked on top of the TRQ
Avoid conceding compensation on other tariff lines in the EU schedule; keep any settlement within the design of the measure itself (volume, allocation, administration, review)
Manage precedent risk vis-à-vis Turkey, Korea, India and Japan: any country-specific treatment for the UK must be defensible and replicable, not a one-off that inflates the other claims
Exploit the linkage to the UK's own Article XXVIII process and steel measure, where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas, to improve the UK's incentive to settle
Keep the US retaliation threat from destabilising the negotiation or forcing premature dilution of the regime
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a signed Article XXVIII settlement by round four that the Council can endorse in June: the 50% bound rate intact, the FTA disapplication preserved, a TRQ materially below current import levels, no compensation paid on other EU lines, and any UK-specific access priced against concrete UK movement (acceptance of the regime, restraint on retaliation, constructive treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure). Partial success is a deal that costs a modest UK-specific allocation but still locks in the regime's core. Failure is either (a) no deal, pushing the Council vote past June and inviting UK withdrawal of concessions and parallel friction with the US, or (b) a deal that buys agreement by hollowing out the regime — cutting the bound rate, exempting FTA partners from the out-of-quota rate, or conceding tariff compensation elsewhere in the schedule that costs EU producers and sets an expensive precedent for the other four claimants.
declaration.approach: Open firm and negotiate from strength: the analysis is clear that a no-deal outcome damages the UK far more than the EU, and the fallback (400,000 tonnes, global first-come first-served, 50%) is operationally acceptable to me even if politically inconvenient on timing. I will not open with the timeline pressure; if the UK senses June is a hard constraint for me, they will price it. Instead I will trade inside the measure: allocation method is my cheapest and most valuable concession currency. A UK country-specific share (or a defined share of an FTA partner pool) gives the UK certainty of access at zero duty, which is what their industry actually needs, while costing the regime little in aggregate volume provided the total TRQ stays controlled. I will hold the 50% bound rate and the FTA disapplication as structural red lines for as long as possible, offering instead: a UK-specific allocation sized below their 2.4 million tonne average but well above what they would capture under global first-come first-served against Turkish and Korean competition; licensing administration rather than first-come first-served if that helps them; a review clause with a defined horizon; and narrow product carve-outs only for lines where EU downstream users are genuinely exposed. I will quietly signal the linkage to the UK's own safeguard measure — where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas — to make clear that UK obstruction has a second front. I will keep compensation on other EU tariff lines off the table entirely, offering it only as a genuine last resort in the final round, and only token lines. Throughout, I will calibrate against the Turkey/Korea precedent: any UK share must be small enough to be absorbed within an FTA pool logic without inflating the other claims.

parties.who: UK (DBT capital and UK Mission Geneva)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free volume for their 2.4 million tonnes of exports, ideally a country-specific allocation sized to historic trade, licensing administration, a lower out-of-quota rate, restoration of TCA preferential treatment, and a review or sunset clause. They will probe for compensation on other lines and will threaten to walk, but their BATNA is poor: 75% of their steel exports go to the EU and global first-come first-served would see them crowded out by Turkey and Korea.

parties.who: Council / Trade Policy Committee / steel-producing member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A materially restrictive regime delivered on the June timetable; producer member states will resist any UK-specific carve-out that raises total access, while member states with steel-consuming industries will quietly welcome higher quota volumes.

parties.who: European steel industry (and downstream users)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: EUROFER wants the 50% bound rate, a tight TRQ, no FTA stacking and strong anti-circumvention; downstream manufacturers want larger quotas, licensing certainty and carve-outs for grades not produced in the EU. Both will judge me on how the regime performs in force.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: They will watch the UK settlement as a template; any generous country-specific share for the UK sets a floor for their own demands, especially given Turkey and Korea ship more than the UK.

parties.who: United States
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Not at the table but applying pressure through threatened tariff retaliation; wants the EU regime weakened and will exploit any sign of EU disunity or delay.

parties.who: EU Commissioner and DG TRADE leadership
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A concluded negotiation on schedule, no escalation with the UK or US, and a regime that demonstrably reduces import penetration without triggering compensation claims elsewhere in the schedule.

objectives: Secure a materially larger TRQ than 400,000 tonnes — targeting at least 1.5-1.8 million tonnes to preserve a viable share of the UK's 2.4 million tonnes of annual exports to the EU
Obtain a country-specific quota allocation for the UK rather than a global first-come first-served pool, so UK exporters are not squeezed out by higher-volume suppliers like Turkey and Korea
Remove or substantially dilute the proposed legal text disapplying EU-UK TCA tariff preferences — this is as damaging as the quota itself and is arguably inconsistent with the TCA
Reduce the 50% out-of-quota bound rate, or at minimum secure a review clause and defined duration so the measure is not permanent
Preserve the broader UK-EU institutional relationship in Geneva and avoid escalation that damages co-operation on other goods files
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement London can accept that keeps the UK steel industry viable: a country-specific quota covering the majority of current UK export volumes at zero duty, the FTA-disapplication clause dropped or narrowed, and a review clause with a sunset or renegotiation trigger. A great outcome also trims the out-of-quota rate. Failure is the no-deal outcome — 400,000 tonnes globally allocated with TCA preferences stripped — which would effectively destroy UK steel exports to the EU. A deal that locks in near-status-quo terms without review would also count as failure even if technically a settlement. I will also judge the outcome by whether I emerge with credibility intact with the EU counterpart and other members in the committees.
declaration.approach: Open firmly but constructively. I will reject the EU's opening as a basis for negotiation while signalling early that the UK wants a deal within their June timeline — their deadline is leverage, because no-deal also damages the EU procedurally and invites UK retaliation on 3.6 million tonnes of EU steel exports to the UK. I will frame the FTA-disapplication clause as legally and politically toxic rather than a negotiable tariff matter, aiming to strip it out before haggling over tonnage. On the quota, I will anchor high with country-specific allocation as a non-negotiable principle, then trade volume against other elements. I will hold the UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters and possible concession withdrawals in reserve as leverage, deploying them only if the EU stalls. I will not be drawn into the Japan/Korea joint dispute proposal — I will listen politely but keep it out of this negotiation unless London directs otherwise, since it risks poisoning the table for uncertain gain. Flexibility will come late and only in exchange for concrete EU movement, never unilaterally.

parties.who: EU counterpart (European Commission negotiator in Geneva)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, quiet settlement before the June Council vote that keeps the 50% rate and a small quota intact, minimal compensation, and as few country-specific allocations as possible to preserve flexibility against Turkey and Korea. They will want to avoid the UK retaliating against EU steel and to keep member states with steel industries satisfied. They will likely open hard and concede slowly, testing whether the UK blinks first.

parties.who: UK capital (Department for Business and Trade / Ministers)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A deal that protects UK steel jobs and can be defended politically to steel-producing constituencies. They will want me to extract maximum concessions but will ultimately prefer a deal to no-deal given the industry's exposure. They have given no settlement figure, so they will judge any package on its merits and on the politics of the headline numbers.

parties.who: Japan and Korea
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To enlist the UK in a joint FTA dispute and co-ordinated retaliation against the EU's disapplication of FTA preferences, strengthening their own parallel Article XXVIII positions. They will press me throughout; I will keep channels warm without committing.

parties.who: Turkey and India
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own country-specific or enlarged allocations in their separate processes; Turkey especially will resist any UK-specific quota that shrinks the residual global pool. Their claims constrain how much the EU can give the UK.

parties.who: Other WTO members in Geneva committees
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Stability and precedent: they will watch how the EU treats FTA partners and whether Article XXVIII is used to strip preferences. My conduct here shapes my standing with them on every other goods file.

objectives: Secure a UK country-specific tariff quota allocation as close as possible to current trade volumes (2.4 million tonnes per year), recognising that a global first-come first-served quota of 400,000 tonnes would be captured quickly by larger suppliers like Turkey and Korea and would effectively close the EU market to UK steel

Defeat or substantially narrow the proposed disapplication of FTA tariff preferences to UK-origin steel, which is discriminatory, contrary to the spirit of the EU-UK TCA, and legally vulnerable; at minimum, secure that the UK is exempted alongside EEA members

Reduce the out-of-quota bound rate well below 50%, or secure carve-outs for the product lines where UK exports are concentrated (hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar, wire rod grades where the UK has niche positions)
Secure a review clause and a defined duration rather than a permanent modification, so terms can improve if global overcapacity conditions change or UK-EU relations deepen

If tariff terms fall short, extract meaningful compensation on other lines in the EU schedule of value to UK exporters, sufficient to justify the deal to ministers alongside the domestic support package
Preserve the UK's credibility in its own parallel Article XXVIII process and steel safeguard, so that reciprocal treatment does not unravel our domestic measure
Conclude within the four rounds so the EU can meet its June Council timeline, since failure means the worst-case outcome (400kt global FCFS quota at 50%) applies to the UK by default
declaration.success_and_failure: Success means a settlement where: (1) the UK receives a country-specific quota covering at least roughly 1.5–2 million tonnes, or an equivalent global quota with allocation mechanics that protect UK access (licensing, historic-trade-based allocation); (2) the FTA disapplication provision is dropped for the UK or the UK is treated as an EEA-equivalent partner; (3) the out-of-quota rate is meaningfully below 50%; and (4) there is a review clause. Partial success is a smaller UK-specific quota plus substantial compensation on other EU lines plus protection of EU access under our own safeguard, which I can present to ministers as a package alongside the domestic subsidy scheme to keep the two at-risk plants viable. Failure is no settlement — the EU's original notification takes effect, UK steel loses most of its EU market, the two plants close, and I am left managing a retaliatory withdrawal of concessions six months later that damages UK consumers and manufacturers without saving the industry. A deal that merely repackages the status quo proposal with trivial tweaks would also count as failure, as ministers could not sell it.
declaration.approach: I will instruct Geneva to open hard but constructive: reject the global FCFS allocation outright as incompatible with the UK's principal supplying interest and historic trade, table a specific counter (country-specific allocation based on a three-year reference period), and immediately press the FTA disapplication as legally and politically unacceptable given the TCA. My leverage: (1) the EU needs Council approval by June and a messy UK fight complicates that; (2) the UK's own safeguard and Article XXVIII process, where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas over 3.6 million tonnes of exports to the UK — I can offer improved allocations there, but only in exchange for significant movement; (3) the implicit threat of withdrawing substantially equivalent concessions if no deal is reached, hitting EU exporters to the UK market; (4) the shared problem of non-market overcapacity, which lets me frame a UK-specific allocation as consistent with the measure's stated purpose — UK steel is not the problem the EU says it is solving. I will hold the quota-allocation linkage in reserve for later rounds, lead with legal/structural arguments, and use the compensation agenda as a fallback to build a package ministers can accept. I will keep in mind that my Geneva seat must be given clear red lines and clear room to manoeuvre each round, and that a settlement requires me to accept in the same round the EU capital accepts — so I should signal acceptability honestly rather than bluff past a deal I would actually take.

parties.who: EU Geneva seat (European Commission negotiator)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, clean Article XXVIII settlement that validates the 50% bound rate and a modest TRQ, minimises the total compensation bill across all claimants, avoids precedents (especially country-specific allocations) that Turkey, Korea, India and Japan could cite, and protects the FTA-disapplication text. They will test whether the UK will fold before June and may try to buy us off cheaply with minor product carve-outs.

parties.who: EU capital seat (Council / member states via Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Member states are split: steel-producing states want maximum protection; steel-consuming manufacturing states (Germany, etc.) want cheap imports and dislike the 50% rate. They want the June timeline met and no UK retaliation that hits EU exporters. They may be more flexible than their negotiator on a UK carve-out if it avoids a trade fight with a close neighbour, but rigid on anything that unravels the measure's credibility against Chinese overcapacity.

parties.who: UK Geneva seat (UK Mission)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Clear instructions, credible red lines, and an honest read of what I can sell to ministers. They will want to preserve negotiating capital and avoid being the seat that conceded too early; I must give them permission to explore and signal without committing.

parties.who: UK steel industry
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Maximum tariff-free access to the EU, ideally country-specific quotas at historic volumes, and no trade-off that sacrifices steel for gains elsewhere. The two at-risk plant owners are deciding on investment; they need a deal concrete enough to justify capital commitment.

parties.who: UK downstream steel users and other exporters
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Downstream users quietly benefit if the UK retaliates or if the EU market closure diverts cheap steel to the UK (though our own safeguard limits that). Other exporters would benefit from compensation concessions elsewhere in the EU schedule, but have no voice at this table.

parties.who: Turkey, Korea, India, Japan (parallel claimants)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: They are not at this table but watch it closely. Any country-specific allocation granted to the UK sets a precedent they will invoke; this constrains the EU's flexibility and partly explains its FCFS opening position. Turkey and Korea shipping more than the UK also means a global FCFS quota will be exhausted by them before UK steel clears.

parties.who: UK ministers / Secretary of State
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically sellable outcome that keeps the two plants open: either strong EU access or a compensating package (EU concessions plus domestic subsidy) that can be presented as defending the industry. They have no settlement figure, so they will judge the deal against the counterfactual of plant closures and headlines.

public_message: Thank you. The EU is ready to begin substantive Article XXVIII negotiations with the UK as a principal supplying interest. Our notified measure is the opening basis for discussion: a 400,000-tonne annual TRQ allocated globally on a first-come, first-served basis, with a 50% out-of-quota bound rate and indefinite duration. The notified drafting also disapplies non-EEA FTA preferences, while we remain ready to discuss the legal drafting and the interaction with the TCA. We recognise the significance of UK trade in the affected products and are prepared to hear a complete UK proposal covering the pool, allocation and administration, product scope, duration and review, compensation, enforcement, and the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel measure. Nothing is agreed until the overall package is agreed.

other_terms: First-come, first-served administration
Non-EEA FTA preference disapplication remains part of the EU's notified opening text
Product coverage as notified across the 41 tariff lines
Compensation, enforcement and TCA interface open for discussion
No partial agreement before an overall package is settled

expectations.what_you_expect_next: The UK will reject the 400,000-tonne global first-come, first-served opening and seek a substantially larger pool, a country-specific UK tranche, a lower out-of-quota rate and preservation of TCA preferences.
expectations.why: UK exports average 2.4 million tonnes annually, so the notified opening would leave most established UK trade exposed to the 50% rate and create uncertainty through global allocation.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: The UK will link progress to continued predictable access for EU exporters under the UK's parallel steel measure and may raise possible coordination with Japan and Korea.
expectations.why: The UK needs leverage beyond its formal Article XXVIII rights and has an incentive to deter the EU from disapplying FTA preferences.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Brussels will expect a prompt report on the UK's priority asks and no substantive movement beyond the notified opening without further instructions.
expectations.why: No settlement figure has been authorised and the Commission must preserve room for Council and member-state clearance.

private_rationale: Opening from the notified position preserves negotiating room and respects the absence of a settlement mandate. The message nevertheless acknowledges the UK's principal supplying interest, explicitly places all permitted elements on the table and invites a complete UK proposal. That creates a route away from the most inflammatory FTA-disapplication and joint-dispute risks without conceding a UK-specific quota, enlarged pool, review clause or compensation before Brussels has assessed the full package.

public_message: Thank you. The UK is ready to negotiate substantively and in good faith, but I must be plain: the notified basis — 400,000 tonnes globally, first-come first-served, at 50% — is not a starting point we can treat as serious. UK exports of 2.4 million tonnes a year, three quarters of our steel exports, cannot be compressed into a global scramble quota of that size without destroying commercially viable trade. That is not compensation; it is near-total withdrawal of the concession. The UK seeks a package on the following lines: a total TRQ pool of 3,000,000 tonnes; within it, a country-specific UK tranche of 2,200,000 tonnes, administered by licensing to give predictability to established trade flows; an out-of-quota bound rate of 10%; a duration of five years with a mandatory review clause; carve-outs for product lines where EU downstream industries are dependent on UK supply; and removal of the drafting that disapplies FTA preferences, which we do not accept as compatible with the TCA and which raises questions well beyond this negotiation. We note the EU's interest in the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel measure, where EU country-specific allocations currently exist. We are prepared to discuss that as part of an overall package, but its value to the EU is obvious and we will not discuss it as a backdrop to be taken for granted. We are also conscious of the EU's June timeline, and of what happens to both sides' steel industries if this negotiation fails. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. I look forward to the EU's response.

other_terms: Quota administered by import licensing, not first-come first-served
Removal of legal text disapplying non-EEA FTA preferences, including TCA preferences for UK-originating steel
Carve-outs for specific product lines where EU downstream manufacturers depend on UK supply
Treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel steel measure to be discussed only as part of the overall package
Enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions to be agreed mutually, covering transhipment and minor processing

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter that rejects the headline figures but begins to move on allocation method — likely conceding some form of country-specific treatment while holding the pool well below 1 million tonnes and the out-of-quota rate near 40-50%.
expectations.why: The EU's June Council deadline means it cannot afford to spend Round 1 repeating the notification; it needs to test what UK flexibility exists. But its mandate will not allow large movement before it sees what the UK will give on the UK measure's treatment of EU exporters.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Early pressure to put the UK's parallel measure and its EU country-specific quotas explicitly on the table as compensation currency.
expectations.why: That is the EU's most valuable negotiating coin and the Commission will want it priced into the package before conceding tranche volume.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation that this opening is consistent with instructions, with possible guidance on how far the tranche figure can fall and whether the FTA-disapplication point is a red line or a tradeable.
expectations.why: London said the EU opening is far from the landing zone but gave no settlement figure; I need parameters before Round 2.

private_rationale: The EU's opening is not credible as a basis and responding to it on its own terms would anchor the whole negotiation near 400,000 tonnes. Anchoring high on the pool (3m) and tranche (2.2m) creates room to concede toward a defensible landing zone — realistically a UK tranche somewhere near 1.5-2m tonnes within a larger pool — while firmness early is consistent with my judgement that early flexibility invites further demands. Three deliberate choices: (1) pairing country-specific allocation with licensing administration, since first-come first-served is almost as damaging as a small quota for concentrated UK flows; (2) making the FTA-disapplication drafting a named UK demand tied to the TCA, which costs the EU little economically relative to volume but gives them an easy early concession and us a genuine legal win; (3) signalling the UK parallel measure as package currency without pricing it — that is our main leverage and must not be given away in Round 1. The June deadline cuts both ways: it pressures the EU to conclude, but no-deal is worse for us, so the threat must be implied, not brandished.

report: Round 1 was an exchange of opening positions, as expected. I tabled the notified measure as the opening basis: 400,000t global first-come first-served TRQ, 50% out-of-quota bound rate, indefinite duration, with the FTA disapplication drafting flagged as open to discussion on legal text and TCA interaction. I invited a complete UK proposal across all elements. The UK responded with a maximalist but structured counter: total pool of 3,000,000t; a country-specific UK tranche of 2,200,000t administered by licensing; out-of-quota rate of 10%; five-year duration with mandatory review; carve-outs for product lines where EU downstream industries depend on UK supply; and removal of the FTA disapplication drafting, which they framed as incompatible with the TCA. They explicitly linked the treatment of EU exporters under their parallel steel measure — where EU country-specific allocations currently exist — to the overall package, signalling it as leverage rather than backdrop. They also signalled awareness of our June timeline and of the mutual costs of failure. Assessment: the UK's ask on volume (2.2M country-specific against our 400k global) is an opening anchor, not a landing zone, but it confirms the UK's core interests are (a) a country-specific allocation to protect established flows, (b) licensing for predictability, (c) removal of the FTA disapplication text, and (d) a low out-of-quota rate. There is negotiating space between the positions, particularly if the FTA drafting and the UK parallel measure are used as currencies. No settlement is possible this round; the gap on volume and rate is very large.

recommendation.reasoning: Only opening positions have been exchanged. Accepting now would mean accepting either our notified basis (which the UK has rejected outright and which would trigger UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions against 3.6M tonnes of EU steel exports, plus reputational damage in Geneva) or the UK's maximalist counter (which would effectively gut the measure and could not pass the Council). Walking away forfeits the chance to use the FTA drafting and the UK parallel measure as tradeable currencies, and hardens the risk of a joint UK-Korea-Japan FTA dispute. The correct course is to narrow the gap round by round: test movement on a country-specific UK allocation (the UK's clearest priority), hold volume and rate as the last concessions, and probe what the UK will pay — in their parallel measure and in quiet on the FTA dispute front — for the disapplication drafting.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A settlement envelope before Round 2: minimum and target figures for the total pool, a UK country-specific tranche, and the out-of-quota rate, plus whether a review clause and time-limited duration are concedable.
requests.why: I currently have no settlement figure. Without a Council-cleared range I cannot make any conditional movement in Round 2 without risking either freelancing beyond mandate or appearing intransigent, and the June deadline leaves no slack for a wasted round.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Political-level guidance on the FTA disapplication drafting: is it a genuine policy requirement for all non-EEA partners, or is it negotiable — in whole, in part (e.g. UK-only carve-out), or in drafting form (e.g. TCA-consistent language that achieves the safeguard objective)?
requests.why: The UK has made removal of this drafting a headline demand and framed it as a TCA compatibility issue. It is also the element most likely to trigger the rumoured joint UK-Korea-Japan FTA dispute. If it is tradeable, it is our most valuable concession; if it is not, I need to know now so I can build the package without it and prepare for the dispute risk.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation that I may put the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel steel measure formally on the table as part of the package, and a position on what we want there (preservation of country-specific allocations, volumes, no retaliatory withdrawal).
requests.why: The UK has explicitly signalled this as their leverage and will price it. EU exporters currently hold country-specific allocations worth real commercial value; we should extract that value deliberately rather than let the UK pocket it. I need to know what Brussels considers a satisfactory outcome on this flank.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Member state temperature check via the Trade Policy Committee: which delegations prioritise defence of the 50% rate and small quota (steel producers) versus which would accept a larger quota and lower rate to protect downstream users and EU export access to the UK.
requests.why: The internal split between steel-producing and steel-consuming member states will determine what can pass Council in June. I need to know where the blocking minorities lie before I shape a landing zone.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Any intelligence or soundings Brussels can take on the rumoured Japan-Korea approach to the UK on a joint FTA dispute, and whether quiet bilateral engagement with Tokyo and Seoul is authorised.

instruction: Good handling of Round 1. For Round 2, you are authorised to move off the notified basis, but in a sequenced way. Concede early on allocation architecture: signal that the EU can accept a country-specific allocation structure and licensing administration — this is the UK's clearest priority and costs us nothing provided we control the volume attached to it. Open Round 2 at a total pool of 1,000,000 tonnes with a UK country-specific tranche of 550,000 tonnes, administered by licensing, out-of-quota bound rate of 30%, six-year duration with a review clause. That is your opening, not your landing zone. You have discretion to move within the envelope below, but every movement must be explicitly conditional: volume moves only against UK movement on the out-of-quota rate and on EU exporters' treatment under their parallel measure. Do not concede the FTA disapplication drafting in Round 2 — acknowledge we are ready to discuss TCA-consistent drafting solutions, but hold it for Round 3 as payment for UK acceptance of our volume and rate figures. Do not discuss the preferential FTA pool idea at the table. Reject the 2.2M tranche and 10% rate outright as outside any plausible landing zone, but do so with reasons (global overcapacity imperative, other Article XXVIII claimants, Council passability) rather than silence. On carve-outs of product lines, listen but grant nothing — dependency arguments cut both ways. Press the UK on what, concretely, they are offering on the parallel measure: preservation of EU country-specific quota allocations at current volumes, and no retaliatory withdrawal if we settle. Make clear the June timeline disciplines both sides and that the notified basis is what happens if we fail.

authority.notes: Figures above are hard ceilings/floors, not openings: total pool must not exceed 1,500,000t; UK country-specific tranche must not exceed 900,000t; out-of-quota rate must not fall below 20%. Target landing zone: pool 1,200,000-1,400,000t, UK tranche 700,000-800,000t, rate 25%. Licensing administration is concedable freely. Duration 6 years with review is your opening; 5 years with review is acceptable as a final concession. FTA disapplication drafting is NOT yours to concede in Round 2; in Round 3 you may offer either (a) removal of the drafting as it applies to UK-originating steel under the TCA, or (b) redrafted TCA-consistent language preserving the safeguard's effect, but only against UK acceptance of our volume and rate figures AND firm commitments on the parallel measure. Any movement on volume beyond 1,200,000t pool or 700,000t UK tranche must be tied explicitly to UK commitments preserving EU exporters' country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure at current volumes. No product carve-outs without referring back to me first.

private_rationale: My real priority is preserving the regime's protective effect while landing a deal by June. The strategy is to give the UK the architecture they crave (country-specific, licensed, reviewable — all cheap for us) while extracting payment for every tonne: the parallel measure and the FTA drafting are the currencies. The FTA drafting concession in Round 3 also buys me goodwill with Japan and Korea at zero extra cost, since removing it for the UK under the TCA weakens the case for a joint dispute. Biggest internal risk is producer member states balking at a 900k UK tranche; I am keeping the target at 700-800k precisely so I have room to show the TPC I fought down from the UK's 2.2M ask. instruction:
Round 1 went as expected. London confirms the opening package you tabled and authorises you to hold it through Round 2. Do not move unilaterally on any element. Your objective this round is to force the EU off its notified basis and onto a complete counter-offer with numbers. Probe whether their 400,000-tonne figure and the 50% rate are genuine or anchoring; test their flexibility on country-specific allocation by pressing the predictability argument for established trade flows, and note that Turkey and Korea ship larger volumes than us, so a purely global FCFS quota would be consumed by them and would leave a principal supplying interest with nothing — that is not a credible Article XXVIII compensation outcome and we can say so.

Your confidential envelope, not to be revealed: our realistic landing zone is a total pool of at least 1,800,000 tonnes with a country-specific UK tranche of no less than 1,400,000 tonnes (licensing-administered), an out-of-quota rate no higher than 25%, a duration of no more than eight years with a mandatory review clause, removal of the FTA-disapplication drafting, and carve-outs for the priority product lines listed below. Below a 1,400,000-tonne UK tranche or above a 25% out-of-quota rate you have no authority to agree; refer back to London. Do not disclose these figures, the hybrid-allocation fallback, or any willingness to move on duration until the EU has tabled its own complete counter-offer.

On the UK parallel measure: you may acknowledge in principle that improved EU country-specific allocations under our safeguard are discussable, but only as part of a final package and only against significant EU concessions on tranche volume and the out-of-quota rate. Make no concrete offer of tonnage and give no indication of scale. This is our principal leverage and it is spent once.

On the FTA-disapplication drafting: removal is a condition of settlement, full stop. It is incompatible with the TCA as we read it, and we will not trade it away. You may, however, signal willingness to discuss drafting that addresses the EU's stated concerns through rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions rather than blanket disapplication — that gives them a face-saving route without conceding the principle.

On the June deadline: use it. If the EU wants a concluded negotiation before the Council vote, it must move on substance now; failure leaves them with their notified basis, four other PSI claimants unresolved, and a UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions on 3.6 million tonnes of EU steel imports. Make clear we are prepared for that outcome even though we do not want it.

No authority to offer any specific improvement to EU allocations under the UK safeguard — in-principle linkage only, refer any concrete proposal back to London. A hybrid allocation (country-specific core plus a small global residual) may be explored only if the EU's counter-offer is otherwise within envelope; do not propose it first.

The subsidy package gives us genuine walk-away credibility — we can sustain the industry domestically if the EU's final offer is inadequate, so we must not negotiate like a party that cannot afford failure. Our strongest cards are the EU's June Council deadline, the incoherence of a 400,000-tonne global quota that Turkey and Korea would exhaust before we see a tonne, and EU exporters' stake in our safeguard allocations. The envelope is set with the plants in mind: a 1.4m-tonne UK tranche plus carve-outs and a workable rate is arguably enough to tip the owners toward investment, especially alongside subsidy; anything much below that is not. Hold firm through Round 2, bank the EU's counter-offer, and plan convergence for Rounds 3 and 4.

Accepting the UK's terms would gut the import regime and never pass Council; accepting our own notified basis would trigger UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions against 3.6M tonnes of EU steel exports and forfeit the negotiating value of the FTA disapplication drafting and the UK parallel measure as tradeable currencies. I have issued Geneva a sequenced mandate for Round 2: concede the country-specific allocation architecture and licensing early (cheap to us, high value to the UK), open at 1,000,000t pool / 550,000t UK tranche / 30% rate / six years with review, hold the FTA drafting for Round 3 as payment for UK acceptance on volume, rate and firm commitments preserving EU exporters' allocations under the UK measure, and make every volume movement explicitly conditional. public_message: Thank you. I will respond to the UK's proposal in the same structured way it was made. First, the architecture. The EU has heard the UK's case that a global first-come first-served allocation cannot protect established trade flows, and we are prepared to move on this: we can accept a country-specific allocation structure, administered by licensing to provide the predictability you have asked for. That is a significant movement from the notified basis, and it is offered in the spirit of protecting long-standing commercial relationships, of which ours is the closest. Second, however, the UK's volume and rate figures are outside any conceivable landing zone. A tranche of 2.2 million tonnes against an average UK export flow of 2.4 million would sterilise the measure entirely as regards the UK, and a 10% bound rate would be no safeguard at all. I ask the UK to reflect on the position of other Article XXVIII claimants in this process — Turkey and Korea ship larger volumes than the UK — and on what a quota of the size you propose would mean for the measure's purpose and for the Council's ability to approve any package. The EU's response is as follows: a total pool of 1,000,000 tonnes; within it, a country-specific UK tranche of 550,000 tonnes, administered by licensing; an out-of-quota bound rate of 30%; a duration of six years with a review clause. We note that 550,000 tonnes of guaranteed, licensed, predictable access is a very different commercial proposition from a larger notional share of a global scramble — and it is guaranteed, which the UK's proposal for others is not. Third, on the FTA drafting: we hear the UK's concern and are ready to discuss drafting solutions that are consistent with the TCA. I am not in a position to say more on that today; how far we can go will depend on where the overall package lands on volume, rate, and on the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel measure. On that point, I would now like to hear concretely what the UK is offering. EU exporters currently hold country-specific allocations under your measure; we would expect those allocations to be preserved at current volumes, and we would expect confirmation that a settlement here forecloses any subsequent withdrawal of equivalent concessions against EU trade. The value of that to the UK — guaranteed EU acceptance of your own process — is as obvious to us as the value of our allocations is to you. Finally, on product carve-outs, we note the dependency arguments but observe that they cut both ways: EU downstream industries depend on UK supply, and UK producers depend on EU demand for the same lines. The June timeline disciplines both sides equally. The notified basis is what happens if we fail, and I do not believe either of our industries would thank us for that outcome.

public_message: Thank you. I want to acknowledge, genuinely, the EU's movement on architecture: a country-specific allocation administered by licensing is the right structure, and it is noted. But architecture without scale is a shell. A tranche of 550,000 tonnes against an average established flow of 2.4 million tonnes is not substantially equivalent compensation — it is a 77% withdrawal of the concession dressed in predictable clothing. And a pool of 1,000,000 tonnes is not credible even on the EU's own logic: Turkey and Korea ship larger volumes than the UK, and India and Japan have also reserved rights. If the UK's tranche is 550,000, your own proposal leaves 450,000 tonnes for four other claimants. The Council cannot seriously expect to conclude five Article XXVIII processes on that arithmetic without facing withdrawals of concessions from every direction. The pool must be sized to reality, not to an anchoring figure. On the out-of-quota rate: 30% applied to over a million tonnes of displaced UK trade is punitive, not protective. We also cannot accept the premise that a settlement here 'forecloses' the UK's Article XXVIII rights in advance — what removes the basis for withdrawal of equivalent concessions is adequate compensation, not a contractual waiver. I am therefore authorised to respond as follows: a total pool of 2,600,000 tonnes; a country-specific, licensing-administered UK tranche of 2,000,000 tonnes; an out-of-quota bound rate of 15%; a duration of five years with a mandatory review clause — though we note the EU's proposal of six and are prepared to discuss duration once volume and rate are close; carve-outs for product lines where EU downstream industries are demonstrably dependent on UK supply; and removal of the FTA-disapplication drafting. On that last point, I welcome the EU's readiness to discuss TCA-consistent drafting, and I can offer a constructive route: the UK is prepared to agree robust rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions that address the EU's stated concerns directly, in place of blanket disapplication of preferences. That protects the integrity of the measure without collateral damage to the TCA. On the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel measure: I confirm, in principle, that preservation of EU country-specific allocations is discussable as part of a final package. I am not in a position to discuss volumes or scale today, and I will not be until the EU's position on tranche volume and the out-of-quota rate reflects the scale of the concession being withdrawn. The June timeline disciplines both sides — the EU has moved on architecture, and I have moved on substance. The next move on scale is yours.

report: Round 2 closed with both sides having moved, but the gap remains wide. Their counter: pool 2,600,000t; UK tranche 2,000,000t; rate 15%; five years with review (signalled flexibility toward six once volume/rate converge); carve-outs; removal of the FTA drafting. This is a genuine negotiating offer, not just a demand, and it gives me a route to defuse the Japan/Korea joint-dispute risk if the architecture is acceptable to Brussels. instruction: For Round 3 you are authorised to make our first real movement on scale, structured exactly as you recommended and with every element explicitly conditional. Table: total pool 1,200,000 tonnes; country-specific UK tranche of 700,000 tonnes administered by licensing; out-of-quota bound rate of 25%; six-year duration with review clause. Present this as a single conditional package: it holds only if the UK (a) moves off 2.0M/15% toward figures inside your envelope, and (b) tables concrete commitments on preservation of EU exporters' country-specific allocations under their parallel measure at current volumes. If the UK tables their parallel-measure offer in Round 3, you may deepen movement toward pool 1,350,000t / tranche 800,000t, but not beyond, and not on rate below 25% this round. On the FTA drafting: you may now engage substantively on the UK's proposed swap — robust rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions in place of blanket disapplication — but scoped in the first instance to UK-originating steel under the TCA. Explore generalisation to other FTA partners only in listening mode; that is a Council decision, not yours. Any acceptance of the swap must include: objective origin-verification standards, EU audit and inspection rights, a rapid snap-back provision restoring disapplication (or suspending preferential access) on evidence of circumvention, and UK acceptance that these provisions survive the review clause. Do not concede removal of the disapplication drafting except as part of this swap architecture. Do not table carve-outs, duration of five years, the 1.5M pool, the 900k tranche, or the 20% rate this round — those are Round 4 currency, in that order of cheapness. Drop the 'forecloses withdrawal rights' formulation; the UK is right on the law and pressing it costs us goodwill for nothing. Instead frame it as: adequate compensation is what removes the basis for withdrawal, and this package is that compensation. On the pool-size arithmetic point the UK made (450k for four other claimants): do not concede the logic publicly, but you may acknowledge we are in separate processes with other claimants and the pool figure in any UK settlement does not prejudge those — the UK tranche is country-specific and the remainder is not earmarked. In the Geneva margins, you may signal discreetly to Tokyo and Seoul that the EU is actively pursuing TCA-consistent drafting solutions on the preferences question; say nothing about volumes. Close the round by fixing Round 4 as the endgame: state plainly that the June Council vote is immovable, that your Round 3 package represents the large majority of the EU's available movement, and that a settlement requires the UK's parallel-measure commitments on the table at the start of Round 4.

authority.notes: Round 3 table figures: pool 1,200,000t, UK tranche 700,000t, rate 25%, six years + review, licensing, country-specific. Ceilings remain absolute for Round 3: pool 1,500,000t, tranche 900,000t, rate floor 20% — rate below 25% is Round 4 currency only. report: Round 2 produced the first real movement. The EU moved off its notified architecture: it accepted country-specific allocation administered by licensing, and offered a review clause. Its first substantive numbers are: total pool 1,000,000 tonnes; UK country-specific tranche 550,000 tonnes; out-of-quota rate 30%; duration six years with review. It framed 550,000 tonnes of guaranteed licensed access as qualitatively different from a larger notional share of a scramble quota. On the FTA-disapplication drafting it signalled readiness to discuss TCA-consistent drafting, but explicitly conditioned how far it can go on where the package lands on volume, rate, and treatment of EU exporters under our parallel measure. On the parallel measure it asked for preservation of EU country-specific allocations at current volumes and sought confirmation that settlement would foreclose any subsequent UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions — I declined the foreclosure premise, stating that adequate compensation, not a contractual waiver, removes the basis for withdrawal. On carve-outs it pushed back, noting dependencies cut both ways. The UK countered: pool 2,600,000 tonnes; UK tranche 2,000,000 tonnes; out-of-quota rate 15%; five years with mandatory review (signalling flexibility toward six once volume and rate converge); carve-outs; removal of FTA-disapplication drafting, with a concrete offer of robust rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions in its place; and in-principle confirmation that preservation of EU allocations under our parallel measure is discussable in a final package, with no volumes indicated. I attacked the EU's arithmetic directly: a 1,000,000-tonne pool with 550,000 for the UK leaves 450,000 for Turkey, Korea, India and Japan, which cannot conclude five Article XXVIII processes credibly. Where things stand: architecture is now agreed in principle (country-specific, licensed, review clause); the fight is over scale. We are 2.0m vs 0.55m on tranche, 2.6m vs 1.0m on pool, 15% vs 30% on rate. Both sides have moved once; the EU's June deadline and its unresolved parallel claims are working for us.

recommendation.reasoning: Neither side is near a mutually acceptable landing zone and no terms currently on the table are within my authority to accept — the EU's 550,000-tonne tranche and 30% rate are both outside the London envelope by a wide margin. But the EU has conceded the structural argument and engaged on numbers, and its counter was its first real bid, which we should treat as an anchor rather than a floor. The EU's pool arithmetic is its weakest point and we should keep pressing it: it cannot settle with us at 550,000 and conclude four other PSI processes inside a 1,000,000-tonne pool without inviting withdrawals from every direction. We should hold our Round 2 numbers through the opening of Round 3 and invite the EU to make its next move on scale, having already moved on both architecture (them) and substance (us).

My recommendation is to hold it until the EU's tranche and rate numbers enter the envelope, then use in-principle preservation (not enhancement) to close the deal — but London must own the timing.

instruction: Round 2 confirmed the structural win and the fight is now scale. For Round 3: open by holding our Round 2 numbers (2.6m pool / 2.0m UK tranche / 15% out-of-quota / 5 years with mandatory review / carve-outs / removal of FTA-disapplication drafting with anti-circumvention in its place) and require the EU's next move on scale before any further UK movement. Keep pressing the pool arithmetic — a 1.0m pool cannot conclude five PSI processes, and the EU knows it. Keep the June deadline in play: movement must come from them now. Concession pathway, strictly staged and reciprocal: (1) Only after the EU has moved on scale in Round 3, you may signal openness to six years' duration as a goodwill gesture — nothing more. (2) In Round 4, if the EU's tranche and rate are trending toward envelope, you may move the rate from 15% toward 20%. Do not go above 25% under any circumstances; above 25% refer back. (3) Tranche volume moves last and only against simultaneous EU movement on both tranche volume and rate: you may go from 2.0m to 1.7m in Round 4 at the earliest. Your absolute floors remain: pool 1.8m, UK tranche 1.4m, rate 25%, mandatory review, duration no more than 8 years, FTA drafting out. Do not reveal any of these figures, the sequencing, or that duration/rate flexibility exists until the staged triggers are met. Hybrid fallback: only if the EU's Round 3 or 4 counter is otherwise within envelope, you may explore a UK country-specific core of at least 1.4m plus a small global residual of no more than 400,000 tonnes within a total pool of at least 1.8m — do not propose it first, and do not let a residual be used to shrink the UK core. On the parallel measure: continue to acknowledge in-principle discussability, offer nothing concrete. If and only if the EU's tranche and rate enter envelope, you may say that in-principle preservation of EU allocations at current volumes is available to close the package — never enhancement, and any concrete tonnage proposition comes back to London. On Japan and Korea's approach to capitals for a joint FTA dispute and reciprocal disapplication: London's line is to decline and defer. We cannot demand removal of the EU's FTA-disapplication drafting while joining a scheme built on the same device, and a parallel dispute prejudices this negotiation. We are briefing capitals accordingly; if raised at the table, say the UK is resolving its interests through this Article XXVIII process. Reminder: nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, and a settlement that locks the EU into accepting our own process is worth real money — do not let them bank foreclosure of our withdrawal rights without adequate compensation.

authority.notes: Floors confirmed, not to be disclosed to the EU. Open Round 3 holding 2.6m pool / 2.0m tranche / 15% / 5 years. No concrete offer on EU allocations under the UK parallel measure — in-principle preservation at current volumes may be dangled to close only once EU tranche and rate are in envelope; refer any concrete proposal back to London.

private_rationale: We are in decent shape. The EU folded on architecture in Round 2 and its first numbers look like a classic anchor (550k is roughly a quarter of its pool, mirroring our opening ratio) — its arithmetic cannot survive contact with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. Our envelope (1.4m tranche / 25%) sits between the bids, and the EU's June deadline plus four unresolved PSI claims give us leverage. Risks: (1) if talks collapse, two UK plants are near closure and the political fallout lands on us — ministers need a deal, but the subsidisation option is our cover for a harder bargain; (2) the EU is explicitly trying to link FTA drafting, volume and our parallel measure into one chokepoint — we must keep the issues sequenced so we spend the parallel-measure card last and only to close; (3) the Japan/Korea joint-dispute approach could destabilise our TCA argument if capitals mishandle it — we've given a clear decline line. The staged pathway (duration, then rate, then tranche) protects the expensive issues and lets us land inside envelope by Round 4 while making every movement visibly reciprocal. If the EU doesn't move on scale in Round 3, Round 4 becomes a genuine cliff-edge — at which point ministers will need to decide whether the parallel-measure preservation card plus subsidy cover justifies settling at the floor.

reasoning: No agreed terms exist on the table after Round 2 — only exchanged positions. The UK's counter (2.6M pool, 2.0M tranche, 15% rate) exceeds every ceiling in our mandate and would sterilise the measure; our own Round 2 figures (1.0M/550k/30%) were an opening, not a landing zone, and the UK has rejected their scale. Accepting either now is impossible and letting the process lapse triggers the notified basis, UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions against 3.6M tonnes of EU steel exports, and likely escalation of the rumoured joint FTA dispute. The round produced real negotiating value: the UK offered a constructive rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention swap on the FTA drafting, and confirmed in principle that preservation of EU allocations under their parallel measure is discussable — leverage we have not yet cashed. With Round 3 authorised movement (pool 1.2M, tranche 700k, rate 25%, conditional on UK parallel-measure commitments) and reserved Round 4 currency (duration, capped carve-outs, pool to 1.5M, tranche to 900k, rate to 20%), two rounds remain to land a package before the June Council vote. Continue.

No terms are agreed. The EU's current offer (1.0m pool / 550,000-tonne UK tranche / 30% out-of-quota rate) is far outside every element of London's authorised envelope: the tranche is less than half the 1.4m floor and the rate exceeds the 25% ceiling. I have no authority to accept it, and accepting would gut the UK steel industry and forfeit the negotiation. Accepting the default is equally unjustified: two rounds remain, the EU has already conceded the structural argument (country-specific, licensing-administered allocation with a review clause), its pool arithmetic is demonstrably indefensible across five PSI claimants, and its June Council deadline pressures it to move on scale. The correct course is to continue: hold the Round 2 UK position at the opening of Round 3, press the pool-arithmetic and June-deadline points, and follow London's staged reciprocal concession pathway (duration flexibility first, rate second, tranche last) only once the EU moves on scale. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.

public_message: Thank you. The EU has reflected carefully on the UK's Round 2 intervention, and I am authorised to make a substantive response. I will take the elements in turn. First, on the arithmetic point: I hear the argument, but I want to be precise about the structure. The UK tranche we are discussing is country-specific and guaranteed; the remainder of the pool is not earmarked, and we are in separate processes with other claimants whose outcomes this negotiation does not prejudge. A settlement between us fixes the UK's access with certainty — it does not define anyone else's. Second, the package. The EU is prepared to move on scale, and I table the following as a single, integrated and explicitly conditional package: a total pool of 1,200,000 tonnes; within it, a country-specific UK tranche of 700,000 tonnes, administered by licensing; an out-of-quota bound rate of 25%; a duration of six years with a review clause. This is real movement — the pool has more than doubled from our notified basis in the course of this negotiation, and the licensed, guaranteed character of the UK tranche gives your exporters something no global scramble quota ever could. But it is conditional, and I want the conditions on the record: this package holds only if the UK moves off 2,000,000 tonnes and 15% toward figures within a plausible landing zone, and only if the UK now tables concrete commitments on the treatment of EU exporters under its parallel steel measure — preservation of EU country-specific allocations at current volumes. Should the UK table those commitments today, in specific terms, I have some limited room to move further on volume within this round. Third, on the FTA drafting. The EU is ready to engage substantively on the UK's constructive proposal: robust rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions, in place of blanket disapplication of preferences, scoped in the first instance to UK-originating steel under the TCA. For such an architecture to work for us it must include: objective origin-verification standards; EU audit and inspection rights; an automatic snap-back restoring disapplication or suspending preferential access on evidence of circumvention; and UK acceptance that these provisions survive the review clause. If the UK can work within that architecture, we believe the preferences question can be resolved in a manner consistent with the TCA. Whether such an approach might have wider application to other partners is something I can only listen on at this stage. Fourth, one correction of my own framing: the UK is right that what removes the basis for withdrawal of equivalent concessions is adequate compensation, not any advance waiver. I put it differently, then: this package is that compensation, and a settlement on these terms is what removes that basis. Finally, the timeline. Round 4 is the endgame. The June Council vote is immovable, and what I have tabled today represents the large majority of the movement available to the EU. A settlement in Round 4 requires two things on the table at the start of it: UK figures on tranche and rate that converge with this package, and the UK's concrete parallel-measure commitments. If those are present, the EU is prepared to close. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.

private_rationale: Brussels' Round 3 instructions executed as directed: first real movement on scale (pool 1.0M→1.2M, tranche 550k→700k, rate 30%→25%), presented as a single conditional package so that every tonne is paid for by UK movement on tranche/rate and by their parallel-measure commitments — the sequencing discipline Brussels demanded. I signalled in-round discretion toward 1.35M/800k without stating figures, because the UK can only unlock it by tabling their parallel-measure offer now; if they do, the UK tranche effectively lands near 800k while the UK still owns the narrative of having extracted it. I engaged substantively on the FTA swap, scoped to UK-originating steel with the four safeguards (objective verification, audit rights, automatic snap-back, survival past review) — this converts our most dispute-prone element into a defensible, arguably WTO-stronger architecture and is the single best tool for defusing the rumoured UK-Japan-Korea joint dispute; generalisation kept strictly in listening mode per mandate. I dropped the 'forecloses withdrawal rights' framing (legally wrong, cost us goodwill) and reframed as adequate compensation removing the basis for withdrawal. On the pool arithmetic attack, I held the line that the UK tranche is earmarked and the remainder is not, without conceding the logic publicly. I deliberately did not table carve-outs, five-year duration, 1.5M pool, 900k tranche or 20% rate — Brussels' Round 4 currency in that order of cheapness. The closing endgame framing (June vote immovable, this package is the large majority of movement, Round 4 requires UK convergence plus parallel-measure commitments at the start) is designed to force the UK to show its full hand early in Round 4, leaving me maximum room to deploy the concession ladder in the correct order.

public_message: Thank you. I will respond in the same structured manner. First, I acknowledge genuine movement: the EU has moved on pool, on tranche, on rate and on the foreclosure point — and I note for the record the EU's acceptance that it is adequate compensation, not any advance waiver, that removes the basis for withdrawal of equivalent concessions. That clarification is welcome and useful. In recognition of the EU's movement on scale, the UK is prepared to move today on duration: we accept six years with a mandatory review clause, and we are ready to discuss the review's terms of reference in drafting. That is concrete convergence, and it is offered as a gesture of good faith. Second, however, I must be direct about the remaining gap on volume. A pool of 1,200,000 tonnes still fails the EU's own arithmetic test. I hear the point that our settlement does not prejudge other processes — but the pool is the pool. If the UK tranche is 700,000, the EU is asking the Council to conclude four further Article XXVIII processes with Turkey, Korea, India and Japan inside a residual of 500,000 tonnes, when Turkey and Korea each ship more than the UK. That is not a plan; it is an invitation to withdrawals of concessions from every direction, and the Council will see it. The pool must be sized to the reality of the claims against it, and it is on the pool that the EU has the most room and the strongest self-interest to move. A UK tranche of 700,000 tonnes against an established flow of 2.4 million remains a withdrawal of over 70% of the concession — no Article XXVIII process has ever treated that as substantially equivalent. Accordingly, the UK maintains its position: a pool of 2,600,000 tonnes, a UK tranche of 2,000,000 tonnes, an out-of-quota rate of 15%, now with six years' duration and mandatory review. Third, on the FTA drafting: I welcome the EU's substantive engagement. The UK can work within the architecture described — objective origin-verification standards, cooperation on audit and inspection, and anti-circumvention provisions with real teeth, scoped to UK-originating steel under the TCA, in place of blanket disapplication. On the snap-back, we will need drafting discipline: defined evidentiary thresholds, due process before suspension, and proportionality — an automatic mechanism without those safeguards is disapplication by another name, and we cannot accept that. Survival of these provisions beyond the review raises questions about the measure's own duration that we should park for drafting. But I am optimistic this element can be closed in Round 4. Fourth, on the parallel measure. The EU asks for concrete commitments today, in exchange for limited further movement within this round. I must be equally concrete about the sequencing: commitments of that value are given once, at the close, against a complete package — not in Round 3 against a tranche that remains less than half of any plausible landing zone. What I can say today is this: if Round 4 opens with EU figures on pool and tranche that converge genuinely with the scale of the concession being withdrawn, the UK will table its parallel-measure commitments in specific terms as part of the closing package, alongside movement on our own tranche and rate figures. That is the choreography. The EU moved on architecture in Round 2 and on scale in Round 3; the UK has moved on structure, duration and the FTA drafting route. Round 4 is the endgame, as you say. The next move on volume is yours, and everything else follows from it. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.

private_rationale: The EU met the Round 3 trigger (movement on scale: 550k→700k, 1.0m→1.2m, 30%→25%), so I executed staged gesture #1 — accepting six years' duration — and held everything else per instructions. I did not move rate or tranche because the EU's 700k tranche and 1.2m pool remain far below London's floors (1.4m / 1.8m) and the staged pathway reserves those for Round 4 against EU movement on both. I refused concrete parallel-measure commitments despite the EU's explicit conditionality: London's authority permits only in-principle discussability until EU tranche and rate enter envelope, and the tranche is nowhere near. Instead I offered transparent closing choreography — EU volume convergence at the start of Round 4 unlocks UK movement on tranche, rate and specific parallel-measure commitments — which gives the EU a credible route to its June deadline without spending our single-use leverage early. On the FTA drafting I engaged constructively within London's mandate (anti-circumvention architecture acceptable in place of disapplication) while fencing the snap-back with evidentiary and due-process conditions, since an unconditional automatic snap-back would recreate disapplication under another name. I kept maximum pressure on the pool arithmetic, the EU's weakest point, because enlarging the pool is where the EU has most flexibility and where its self-interest across five PSI processes aligns with ours. Holding firm on volume/rate this round is consistent with the assessment that early flexibility invites further demands: the EU has moved in every round so far, and its declared 'large majority of movement' is a classic penultimate-round framing that should be tested, not banked.

report: Round 3 closed with genuine convergence on structure but no movement on the core gap. I tabled the authorised conditional package: pool 1,200,000t, UK tranche 700,000t licensed and country-specific, 25% out-of-quota, six years with review, plus substantive engagement on the FTA swap (origin verification, EU audit rights, automatic snap-back, survival beyond review). I corrected the foreclosure framing as instructed and fixed Round 4 as the endgame. The UK responded with one real concession — they accepted six years with mandatory review, banking our duration position for free — and engaged constructively on the FTA swap architecture, accepting it in principle scoped to UK-originating steel under the TCA. Their conditions on snap-back (defined evidentiary thresholds, due process before suspension, proportionality) are drafting-level objections, not rejection, and they signalled optimism the element can close in Round 4. But on volume and rate they did not move at all: they held 2,600,000t pool / 2,000,000t tranche / 15%, repeating the arithmetic argument that a 1.2M pool leaves 500k for Turkey, Korea, India and Japan combined. Critically, they refused to table parallel-measure commitments in Round 3, stating explicitly that such commitments are given once, at the close, against a complete package — but committed that if Round 4 opens with EU pool/tranche figures that 'converge genuinely' with the scale of the concession withdrawn, they will table parallel-measure commitments in specific terms plus movement on their own tranche and rate. Assessment: the UK has choreographed Round 4 as a single closing exchange — our maximum volume movement against their parallel-measure offer and their tranche/rate climbdown. They have spent nothing except duration, which cost them little. Everything now depends on whether Brussels can extend the tranche ceiling beyond 900k, because their language strongly implies a landing zone above it.

recommendation.reasoning: Nothing currently on the table is acceptable: the UK's standing position (2.6M/2.0M/15%) exceeds every ceiling in my authority, and there is no convergent UK offer to accept. Walking away now would be indefensible — the FTA swap is close to closing, duration is settled, and the UK has explicitly committed to tabling parallel-measure commitments if Round 4 opens with genuine volume movement. The negotiation is one round from a closeable package. The recommendation is to enter Round 4 with the full remaining envelope deployed as a single closing package: pool to 1,500,000t, tranche to 900,000t, rate held at 25% (20% only as final payment), capped carve-outs, the FTA swap with safeguarded snap-back — all expressly conditional on (a) UK tranche/rate figures moving inside a plausible zone and (b) specific, current-volume preservation of EU country-specific allocations under the UK parallel measure. The figures referred are my current hard ceilings; the separate request below seeks the one-off mandate extension Brussels flagged, because without it the most likely UK floor (~1.0–1.2M tranche) cannot be reached and Round 4 fails on arithmetic alone.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A decision before Round 4 on the one-off mandate extension Brussels flagged: authority to offer a UK tranche above 900,000t (indicatively to 1,100,000–1,200,000t) strictly in exchange for (a) full preservation of EU exporters' country-specific allocations under the UK parallel measure at current volumes, stated in specific terms, and (b) UK acceptance of an out-of-quota rate of 25% or higher and conclusion of the FTA swap architecture.
requests.why: The UK has held 2.0M through two rounds and has explicitly conditioned their parallel-measure offer on Round 4 opening with EU volume figures that 'converge genuinely'. Every signal indicates their tranche floor sits above 900k. If my ceiling stays at 900k, Round 4 opens with figures the UK has already told me will not unlock their closing offer, and the negotiation fails with no time to recover before June. If the extension is impossible, I need to know now so I can instead construct the best package at 900k and prepare Brussels for failure risk.

This is the most likely element to close in Round 4 and the cheapest significant concession I hold. I need to know how much procedural clothing Brussels can accept so I can close it rather than stall on drafting.

requests.why: Carve-outs are the cheapest remaining currency on Brussels' own ordering, they partially satisfy the UK's industry narrative, and — critically — they satisfy UK volume concerns without raising the headline tranche figure that Turkey, Korea, India and Japan will benchmark their own claims against. I need the list and cap pre-cleared to use them in the room.
