If Tokyo and Seoul still believe blanket disapplication is coming for them, the joint-dispute risk survives an EU-UK settlement. I need to know whether a further signal — that generalisation to other partners is under active Council consideration — is authorised, since that is the single most effective step to de-fuse the rumoured joint action.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Fallback instruction: if Round 4 fails, confirmation that the notified basis proceeds as drafted, and whether Brussels wants a final without-prejudice session after the formal rounds to attempt a political close before the June vote.
requests.why: I need to be able to state the consequence of failure credibly at the start of Round 4, and to know whether there is any procedural slack after the formal endgame before the Council vote.

private_rationale: The UK has played this well: they banked our duration position for nothing, spent nothing on volume or rate, and have choreographed Round 4 so that our maximum volume movement is the price of merely seeing their parallel-measure offer. I should not pretend otherwise to Brussels. But the structural reality favours a deal: they need settlement before June as much as we do — failure leaves their steel industry facing 400k global first-come first-served access, which is far worse for them than our worst case is for us. My honest assessment of the landing zone: pool 1.4–1.5M, UK tranche 1.0–1.1M, rate 20–25%, six years with review, UK-scoped FTA swap with a procedurally safeguarded snap-back, capped carve-outs, and EU allocations preserved at current volumes under their measure. That is above my current tranche ceiling, which is why the mandate extension request is the pivotal item — if Brussels holds 900k, we almost certainly fail, and I should quietly prepare the ground for the fallout with Japan and Korea in that case. I have not told Brussels that the UK's six-year acceptance was effectively free — actually I have, it's in the report; but what I have not said is that I judge the UK capital seat may accept a tranche below 1.0M if the carve-outs and swap are generous enough, so the extension should be treated as a ceiling to approach, not a target to open at. Open Round 4 at pool 1.35M / tranche 850–900k with the full conditional architecture, and make them climb to meet us.

report: Round 3 produced real EU movement but the package remains well outside my authority. The EU said that if we table those commitments in specific terms, it has limited room to move further on volume within the round — and that what it has tabled represents 'the large majority' of available movement, with Round 4 as the endgame. On the FTA drafting, the EU engaged substantively on our anti-circumvention route in place of blanket disapplication, scoped to UK-originating steel under the TCA, but with conditions: objective origin-verification standards, EU audit and inspection rights, an automatic snap-back restoring disapplication on evidence of circumvention, and survival of these provisions beyond the review clause. I accepted that architecture in principle while reserving on snap-back drafting (evidentiary thresholds, due process, proportionality) and parking the survival question. Significantly, the EU withdrew its foreclosure framing and accepted on the record that adequate compensation, not an advance waiver, removes the basis for withdrawal of equivalent concessions — a useful clarification that protects our Article XXVIII rights in any settlement. Where things stand: duration (6 years), review clause, licensing, country-specific structure and the FTA drafting route are all effectively converged. The entire remaining fight is pool and tranche volume, with the rate at 25% (our ceiling) as the EU's current bid against our 15%. The EU has made our parallel-measure card the explicit key that unlocks further volume movement — it must be played at the opening of Round 4 or there will be no further EU movement at all.

public_message: Thank you. Round 4 is the endgame, and I will open it as such. The June Council vote is immovable. What I table now is the EU's closing package — the full extent of the movement available to this delegation — and every element of it is explicitly conditional. First, the package itself: a total pool of 1,500,000 tonnes; within it, a country-specific UK tranche of 900,000 tonnes, administered by licensing, guaranteed and predictable; an out-of-quota bound rate of 25%; a duration of six years with a mandatory review clause, as the UK has already accepted. In addition, the EU is prepared to agree a defined list of product-line carve-outs for lines with demonstrated EU downstream dependency on UK supply, capped at 100,000 tonnes per year within the pool — this responds directly to the case the UK has made since Round 1 and does so without disturbing the tranche structure. Second, on the FTA drafting: the EU confirms the swap architecture scoped to UK-originating steel under the TCA — robust rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions in place of blanket disapplication. On the snap-back, we have heard the UK's drafting concerns and can accept procedural clothing: defined evidentiary thresholds, a consultation window of no more than ten working days before any suspension, and proportionality in application. What we cannot accept is prior external review as a precondition — the mechanism must be rapid, evidence-triggered, and reviewable in arrears, or it is no safeguard at all. On that basis I believe this element can be closed today. Third, the conditions, and I want them on the record with complete clarity. This package holds only if the UK now tables, in specific terms: its convergent figures on tranche and rate, and its commitments on the treatment of EU exporters under the UK's parallel steel measure — preservation of EU country-specific allocations at current volumes. The UK told this table in Round 3 that if Round 4 opened with genuine movement on volume, those commitments would be forthcoming in specific terms, alongside movement on the UK's own figures. The EU has now moved: the pool is nearly four times the notified basis, the tranche has nearly doubled since Round 2, the rate has fallen, the carve-outs are tabled, and the preferences question has a closed architecture. I will be equally plain about what remains: if the UK tables specific current-volume preservation commitments, accepts an out-of-quota rate of 25%, and concludes the swap architecture, I have strictly limited room to move further on the UK tranche — and that room is exhausted by that movement. There is nothing behind it. A tranche above that level cannot pass the Council, and no referral from this room will change that. On the residual pool, I repeat: our processes with other claimants are separate and are not prejudged by this settlement; the remainder is not earmarked. On the question of wider application of the swap architecture to other partners, I can say only that it is under active consideration at political level. Finally, the consequence of failure, stated once and without pleasure: the notified basis proceeds — 400,000 tonnes, globally allocated, first-come first-served, at 50%. The UK loses guaranteed licensed access entirely; the carve-outs, the swap, the tranche all disappear; and the costs to UK steel are severe and immediate, as they are to EU exporters facing withdrawal of equivalent concessions. Neither industry deserves that outcome, and it is avoidable today. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed — but everything can be agreed today.

public_message: Thank you. The UK will respond in the same endgame spirit, and I will begin by honouring the choreography I set out in Round 3. First, the parallel measure. I am authorised to state, in specific terms: as part of a concluded package, and for so long as the EU measure remains in force, the United Kingdom will preserve EU country-specific allocations under the UK's parallel steel measure at current volumes. That is a concrete, current-volume preservation commitment. It is not enhancement; it is not an advance waiver of Article XXVIII rights — and I note the EU has accepted on the record that it is adequate compensation, not any waiver, that removes the basis for withdrawal. It becomes operative only on conclusion of the full package and only if the package meets the UK's conditions. It is on the table now, as promised. Second, the FTA drafting. The UK accepts the swap architecture as described: rules-of-origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions scoped to UK-originating steel under the TCA, in place of blanket disapplication, with defined evidentiary thresholds, a ten-working-day consultation window before any suspension, and proportionality in application. I ask for two additions in drafting, both modest: express provision for restoration of preferential access once the triggering conduct is cured, and confirmation that these provisions run co-terminously with the measure as confirmed through the review, rather than surviving it indefinitely on a standalone basis. With those, this element is closed. Third, the carve-outs: welcomed, additive, and we will table the dependency evidence in drafting. Fourth, scale — the one remaining issue, and the one on which everything now turns. The UK moves today: we accept an out-of-quota bound rate of 25%, and we move our tranche figure to 1,700,000 tonnes. And I offer the structure that closes this: a guaranteed, country-specific, licensing-administered UK core of 1,400,000 tonnes, within a total pool of 1,800,000 tonnes, with the remainder available as a global residual on which UK exporters may also draw. This gives the Council a measure that bites — a binding 25% bound rate on out-of-quota trade, a global residual, carve-outs capped as you propose — while giving a principal supplying interest with 2.4 million tonnes of established flow a guaranteed core that is still a substantial concession withdrawal. The EU has told this table it retains limited room on the tranche, unlocked by the commitments I have now tabled. Those commitments are tabled. The rate the EU asked for is accepted. The structure that bridges us is proposed. I ask the EU to use the full extent of its remaining room, now, on the core and the pool. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed — and everything can still be agreed today.

report: Round 4 closed with the UK honouring its Round 3 choreography and tabling its closing offer, but the numbers remain outside my absolute authority. The UK delivered three of the four things we demanded: (1) a specific, on-the-record commitment to preserve EU country-specific allocations under its parallel steel measure at current volumes, operative on conclusion of the full package and for so long as the EU measure remains in force; (2) acceptance of the 25% out-of-quota bound rate; (3) acceptance of the FTA swap architecture — origin enforcement and anti-circumvention provisions scoped to UK-originating steel under the TCA, with defined evidentiary thresholds, a ten-working-day consultation window, and proportionality. They asked only for two modest drafting additions: express restoration of preferential access once triggering conduct is cured, and swap provisions running co-terminously with the measure as confirmed through review (rather than surviving it indefinitely). Both are within the drafting latitude you gave me. On scale, they moved hard but not far enough: from 2.0M tranche to a structured proposal of a guaranteed, licensed, country-specific UK core of 1,400,000t within a total pool of 1,800,000t, with the remainder a global residual on which UK exporters could also draw. This exceeds my absolute ceiling (1,100,000t tranche / 1,500,000t pool) by 300,000t on both variables. I did not deploy the 1,100,000t extension in the room — the conditions for it (25% acceptance, specific preservation commitments, swap conclusion) were only tabled at the close, and their tranche demand sits above the extension ceiling, so there was nothing I could put against it without freelancing. The negotiation state: everything is closed or closeable except 300,000t of tranche and 300,000t of pool. The UK has spent its parallel-measure commitment, its rate position, and the swap. The residual global-draw element of their proposal is a genuine structural bridge — it lets them argue effective access above the core without us benchmarking a headline tranche of 1.4M to Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. Failure now means the notified basis (400k global FCFS at 50%), UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against 3.6M tonnes of EU steel exports within six months, near-certain collapse of goodwill on the Japan/Korea joint-dispute front, and loss of the parallel-measure preservation we have extracted — which exists only as part of a concluded package.

Walking away is indefensible with the package this close — 300,000t separates us on each variable, every other element is settled or in drafting, and failure triggers the worst outcome for EU exporters, the Geneva goods file, and the wider FTA-partner dispute risk. The correct course is to hold our maximum authorised package — 1,500,000t pool, 1,100,000t licensed country-specific UK tranche, 25% out-of-quota rate, six years with mandatory review, 100,000t capped carve-outs, concluded FTA swap with the UK's two drafting additions — and put it to the UK as the Council's final word, while using the decision phase and any residual window before the June vote to attempt a political close. instruction: The formal rounds are exhausted but the negotiation is not over: you are authorised to seek a political close in a without-prejudice session before the June Council vote. Approach the UK immediately and put the following as the EU's final, integrated, take-it-or-leave-it package, sequenced as follows. STEP ONE: offer a total pool of 1,800,000 tonnes, with the UK core tranche held at 1,100,000 tonnes, licensed and country-specific, at 25% out-of-quota — emphasising that the enlarged residual of 700,000 tonnes is global and unearmarked, that UK exporters may draw on it, and that this structure gives the UK effective access toward the very figure they tabled while keeping the guaranteed core at a level that does not set a country-specific benchmark for Turkey, Korea, India and Japan. Present the pool movement from 1.5M to 1.8M as the EU bridging the full 300,000-tonne gap on the variable that costs the measure least. STEP TWO: if and only if the UK confirms it will close on this basis except for the core, you may move the UK core to a maximum of 1,200,000 tonnes — state explicitly that this is beyond any mandate previously given, that it required a one-off political decision, and that there is nothing behind it. STEP THREE: the 20% out-of-quota rate is your absolute final payment, released only to close a complete package that includes: the specific current-volume parallel-measure preservation commitment as tabled in Round 4, the concluded FTA swap architecture with the safeguarded snap-back, and UK acceptance of everything else as settled. Do not trade the rate against anything else. On the swap: you may accept both UK drafting additions — express restoration of preferential access on cure of the triggering conduct, and co-terminous running with the measure as confirmed through review. Both are within existing latitude and cost nothing. On the parallel-measure commitment: the mutual conditionality the UK tabled (operative on conclusion, for so long as our measure remains in force) is acceptable; seek preservation at current volumes only, no enhancement, and mirror the conditionality in the package text. On the residual pool: hold the line that it is not earmarked and that our processes with other claimants are not prejudged — do not accept any drafting that allocates it. Duration stays at six years with mandatory review; the 100,000-tonne capped carve-out list stands as tabled within the pool. In the Geneva margins you are authorised to signal discreetly to Tokyo and Seoul that generalisation of the swap architecture to other FTA partners is under active consideration at political level — nothing more, nothing on volumes. If the UK will not close on these terms, tell them plainly that the notified basis proceeds, the parallel-measure commitment and the swap lapse with the package, and the consequences for UK steel are severe and immediate. Report the outcome the same day; the Commissioner and the Trade Policy Committee are being briefed on the final package in parallel.

authority.notes: Hard ceilings for the political close: pool 1,800,000t; UK core tranche 1,200,000t; rate floor 20%. Sequencing is mandatory: (1) open at pool 1,800,000t with core held at 1,100,000t and 25%; (2) release core to 1,200,000t only if the UK confirms it will otherwise close; (3) release the 20% rate only as the final element against the complete package — specific current-volume parallel-measure preservation, concluded FTA swap with safeguarded snap-back, six years with mandatory review, capped carve-outs (100,000t/yr, within the pool). The residual pool is global, unearmarked and must not be allocated in drafting; UK exporters may draw on it competitively but it is not guaranteed access. Swap drafting: accept restoration-on-cure and co-terminous running; snap-back remains rapid and evidence-triggered with a maximum ten-working-day consultation window, no prior external review. No enhancement of the parallel-measure commitment beyond current volumes; mutual conditionality acceptable. Nothing agreed until everything agreed. If no close: the notified basis proceeds.
